name: Tunisia
summary_text: Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women. In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.

sources.title: Tunisia: Authorities step up crackdown on LGBTI individuals with wave of arrests - Amnesty International
sources.claim_summary: Amnesty International (Feb 2025): Tunisia steps up crackdown on LGBTI individuals with a wave of arrests - at least 84 people (mainly gay men and trans women) arrested, arbitrarily detained and unjustly prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, solely based on actual or perceived SOGI, per Damj Association.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying Middle East Eye piece covered the same Tunisian crackdown arrests.

sources.title: Tunisia | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 country review of Tunisia: gender identities/expressions deviating from norms are effectively criminalised via Penal Code Articles 226 bis and 230, disproportionately targeting trans women; no comprehensive legal gender recognition framework - inconsistent rulings relying on judges' personal views and Sharia interpretations; gender-affirming care accessible only through well-informed medical professionals.

sources.title: Transgender Women In Tunisian prisons: continuous suffering and significant challenges - جمعية تقاطع
sources.claim_summary: Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons endure continuous suffering - processed under former names and gender identification in all official procedures; forced shaving on entry without consent causes profound psychological harm, targeting the essence of their gender identity.

sources.title: Tunis Court of First Instance: Gender Identity Disorder is Not A Valid Reason for Legal Gender Recognition | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 (Jan 2024): the Tunis Court of First Instance (April 2023) declined legal gender recognition to a trans man, asserting insufficient evidence of a biological medical condition and dismissing gender identity disorder as a mental illness not fulfilling LGR criteria - reasoning based on comparative law from Egypt, ECtHR case-law and Dar Al-Ifta religious opinions.

sources.title: Tunisia: Men Prosecuted for Homosexuality | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: HRW (March 2016): 'Tunisia: Men Prosecuted for Homosexuality' - documents prosecutions under Article 230 and the use of forced anal examinations as 'evidence'.

sources.title: GayLawNet®™ | Laws | Tunisia | TN
sources.claim_summary: GayLawNet laws page for Tunisia: the 2012 draft bill punishing 'insulting the sanctity of religion'; courts refused to ban the LGBT radio station Shams Rad (2018) and upheld Shams's right to exist (2019) against government shutdown efforts.

sources.title: Tunisia drops anal tests, but not its anti-gay law
sources.claim_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing (minister Mehdi Ben Gharbia in Geneva) but did not accept repeal of Article 230 (up to 3 years); Shams president Mounir Baatour was unenthusiastic - the abusive 'test' was dropped but the law remains.
